explanations.explanation: That's the message, friend. The envoy says, “Rise up, and let us go to battle against her!” (Obadiah 1:1). The "her" is Edom. Getting a message from the LORD that starts with "Rise up" is not the kind of mail you leave unopened.
No pens and no handshakes on this one. The envoy's message is a call to go to battle against Edom. Nobody is bringing a treaty to sign. I think Edom would have preferred the paperwork.

No gift bags and no welcome committee here. The envoy says, “Rise up, and let us go to battle against her!” (Obadiah 1:1). That's a call to battle, not a card with a bow on it. Edom is getting the opposite of a present.

Right on the money, baker. The LORD says, “The pride of your heart has deceived you…” (Obadiah 1:3). Nobody else had to fool Edom, because its own heart did the job. When you're the one telling yourself the story, you're a very easy audience.

That's a fair guess, but the text doesn't mention false prophets here. The LORD points inward: “The pride of your heart has deceived you…” (Obadiah 1:3). The voice doing the deceiving was Edom's own. I think that makes it sneakier.

Idols never come up in this verse. It says Edom lives in the clefts of the rocks, up on the heights, and what deceived them was “The pride of your heart…” (Obadiah 1:3). The trouble was in their own heart. Nobody had to carve it out of anything.

True! The LORD says, “Though you soar like the eagle and make your nest among the stars, even from there I will bring you down,” (Obadiah 1:4). Edom could go as high as an eagle and then keep climbing. The LORD says the height doesn't matter. Higher than the stars still isn't out of His reach.

It's actually true. The LORD says, “Though you soar like the eagle and make your nest among the stars, even from there I will bring you down,” (Obadiah 1:4). Edom could nest up among the stars and the LORD would still bring them down. That's one very tall nest.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, “But how Esau will be pillaged, his hidden treasures sought out!” (Obadiah 1:6). Thieves and grape gatherers would leave something behind. Esau's treasures, hidden away or not, get searched out.

That's the opposite of what the LORD says. Thieves might take only what they wanted, but for Esau the LORD says, “But how Esau will be pillaged, his hidden treasures sought out!” (Obadiah 1:6). Hidden treasures don't stay hidden here. Somebody is going to be digging.
Nobody is handing anything out. The LORD says Esau will be pillaged and his hidden treasures sought out (Obadiah 1:6). That's taking, not giving. I'd call it a very unfriendly yard sale.

That's the one. “Those who eat your bread will set a trap for you without your awareness of it.” (Obadiah 1:7). These are people Edom shared a table with. Edom had no idea what was coming, and that's the part that stings.

I see why you'd pick it, since we're talking about eating bread. But the verse says those who eat Edom's bread “will set a trap for you…” (Obadiah 1:7). Nobody is throwing Edom a party. Sharing a table and then getting trapped is a rough way to end a meal.

Close to the idea of watching, but no guard is set here. The verse says those who eat Edom's bread “will set a trap for you without your awareness of it.” (Obadiah 1:7). A guard protects, and a trap does the opposite. Edom doesn't see it coming.

That's the other way around, friend. The LORD asks, “In that day, declares the LORD, will I not destroy the wise men of Edom and the men of understanding in the mountains of Esau?” (Obadiah 1:8). The wise men aren't saving anything here. All that wisdom doesn't hold up in that day.

False is right. The LORD says He will destroy the wise men of Edom and the men of understanding in the mountains of Esau (Obadiah 1:8). They don't save the mountains. Being the smartest ones in the room doesn't help when the LORD has spoken.

You got it. The LORD says, “Then your mighty men, O Teman, will be terrified…” (Obadiah 1:9). Even the strongest people in Teman, the ones everybody counts on, are shaking. I'm just glad nobody asked me to be the mighty man.

Mighty men do sound like they'd stand firm, I'll give you that. But the LORD says, “Then your mighty men, O Teman, will be terrified…” (Obadiah 1:9). Standing firm isn't in the picture. Their muscles don't help them here.
No victory for them in this verse. The LORD says the mighty men of Teman “will be terrified…” (Obadiah 1:9). Terrified fighters aren't winning anything. This is a heavy part of the vision.

That's the reason, baker. The LORD says, “Because of the violence against your brother Jacob, you will be covered with shame and cut off forever.” (Obadiah 1:10). Jacob was Edom's own family, and that makes the hurt go deeper. This is a heavy verse.

Idols aren't mentioned here. The reason is stated plainly: “Because of the violence against your brother Jacob…” (Obadiah 1:10). The LORD points to how Edom treated family. That's the whole case in this verse.
Not quite. Verse 11 does say Edom stood aloof while strangers carried off Jacob's wealth. But the reason in verse 10 is “Because of the violence against your brother Jacob…” (Obadiah 1:10).

True. The LORD says, “On the day you stood aloof while strangers carried off his wealth and foreigners entered his gate and cast lots for Jerusalem, you were just like one of them.” (Obadiah 1:11). Edom didn't have to carry anything off to be counted with them. Standing on the sidelines still put Edom in that crowd.

It's true, actually. The LORD says Edom stood aloof while strangers carried off Jacob's wealth, and then says, “…you were just like one of them.” (Obadiah 1:11). Standing aloof wasn't a neutral spot. The LORD puts Edom right alongside those strangers.

That's the one. The LORD says, “But you should not gloat in that day, your brother’s day of misfortune, nor rejoice over the people of Judah in the day of their destruction…” (Obadiah 1:12). Judah's hard day was no day for cheering. A neighbor's worst day isn't a party.

Ruling isn't what the verse says. It says Edom should not “rejoice over the people of Judah in the day of their destruction…” (Obadiah 1:12). The word is rejoice. Cheering at someone else's loss is the problem.

Trampling doesn't show up in this verse. The LORD says Edom should not “rejoice over the people of Judah in the day of their destruction…” (Obadiah 1:12). The word is rejoice. The LORD says that day was no time for celebrating.

You got it. The LORD says Edom should not “loot their wealth in the day of their disaster.” (Obadiah 1:13). Looting is one of the things on His list. Taking advantage of somebody's worst day is the whole problem.

Burning houses isn't on this list. In verse 13 the LORD says Edom should not enter the gate of His people, gloat over their affliction, or “loot their wealth in the day of their disaster.” Looting is the one you're looking for.

Tearing down walls isn't in the verse. The LORD lists entering the gate of His people, gloating over their affliction and looting their wealth, all “in the day of their disaster.” (Obadiah 1:13). Looting is the one on the card.

True. The LORD says, “Nor should you stand at the crossroads to cut off their fugitives…” (Obadiah 1:14). Those fugitives were people trying to get away. A crossroads is where they'd be heading, and Edom shouldn't be waiting there.

It's true. The LORD says, “Nor should you stand at the crossroads to cut off their fugitives, nor deliver up their survivors in the day of their distress.” (Obadiah 1:14). People who were trying to escape shouldn't have found Edom standing in their way.

explanations.answer: What they did will be done to them
explanations.explanation: That's it. The LORD says, “As you have done, it will be done to you; your recompense will return upon your own head.” (Obadiah 1:15). Edom's actions come back around. Same measure, same direction.

explanations.answer: They will be spared and forgiven
explanations.explanation: The text says something else. Right after "the Day of the LORD is near," the LORD tells Edom, “As you have done, it will be done to you…” (Obadiah 1:15). Nothing about being spared in this verse. What Edom did is what comes back.

explanations.answer: They will rule over the nations
explanations.explanation: No ruling for Edom here. The LORD says, “As you have done, it will be done to you; your recompense will return upon your own head.” (Obadiah 1:15). That points toward what they did, not toward a throne.

It's the other way around, friend. The LORD says, “But on Mount Zion there will be deliverance, and it will be holy, and the house of Jacob will reclaim their possession.” (Obadiah 1:17). Reclaim means they get it back. The house of Jacob isn't losing it for good.

False is right. The LORD says there will be deliverance on Mount Zion, and “the house of Jacob will reclaim their possession.” (Obadiah 1:17). They get it back. That's good news after all those hard verses.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, “…but the house of Esau will be stubble—Jacob will set it ablaze and consume it.” (Obadiah 1:18). The house of Jacob is the fire, and the house of Esau is the stubble. That's the picture the LORD paints.

Stone is a tough thing to set on fire, so it doesn't fit the picture. The LORD says the house of Esau will be stubble, and “Jacob will set it ablaze and consume it.” (Obadiah 1:18). Jacob's house is the fire and Esau's is what it burns. The word is stubble.

Water isn't the picture here. The LORD says the house of Jacob will be a blazing fire and the house of Esau will be stubble. Then, “Jacob will set it ablaze and consume it.” (Obadiah 1:18). Stubble is what burns.

That's the last line of the whole vision, baker. “And the kingdom will belong to the LORD.” (Obadiah 1:21). After the mountains, the fire and the list of lands, the final word is about whose kingdom it is. It's the LORD's.

Edom had a lot of height and a lot of pride, but it isn't the answer. The vision ends with “And the kingdom will belong to the LORD.” (Obadiah 1:21). The deliverers rule over the mountains of Esau, and the kingdom still belongs to the LORD.
The nations show up in this vision, but the kingdom isn't theirs. The last line says, “And the kingdom will belong to the LORD.” (Obadiah 1:21). The final word goes to the LORD.
